new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for kach1284, so this is a new statement. It describes the Ganta/Kachama variety, and is compatible with Hirut 2004 on Haro: one culminative H per simple word, penultimate or final, lexically fixed; Semu is less committal on type (declines 'tonal or not') where Hirut says 'tone-accent language'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ganta (the variety the older literature calls Kachama) has one high tone per simple word, marked with an acute; in simple nouns it sits on the final mora (moló 'fish', kaná 'dog', maaʔó 'cloth') or on the penultimate mora (kútʃe 'hand', ʔálʔo 'expensive'), and which of the two is lexical; the single trisyllabic example has it on the antepenult. The author explicitly declines to classify the system as tone or accent. High tone shifts under affixation (definite forms, derivation, infinitive), is fixed per paradigm in verbs, and distinguishes lexical items (káɸo 'guarding' vs kaɸó 'bird', p. 75) and grammatical categories (adessive/inessive -á). No word 'stress' is used for Ganta itself; the term appears only in the Azeb (1996) chart of Omotic prosodic types (Wolaitta once 'stress', now 'tonal-accent'), p. 66.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. More than one high tone per word occurs in reduplicated ideophones (h-tʃi h-tʃi 'calling for dog', p. 68), two-noun indefinite pronouns (p. 67), compounds keep H on the first component only (p. 74); numerals 'five' and 'nine' carry H on two vowels (p. 72).
new_statements.exceptions: Author refuses to decide tonal vs accentual; simple demonstratives so/ha carry no H; head nouns lose H after numerals and adjectives in NPs (p. 72-73); postpositions drop H beside a noun (p. 74); instrumental/perlative/inessive suffixes do not shift H while other suffixes do (p. 70). Text-layer caveat: extracted text drops acute-accented vowels, '(', '8' and 'z' from this PDF; the example forms above were verified from page images (PDF 85, 93).
new_statements.identity_note: Hirut 2004 describes Haro (also Haruro; Fleming's 'Geditcho'), spoken on Gidicho island in Lake Abaya; the author reports it mutually intelligible with Ganjule and Gatsame (Kachama) per Haro elders (p. 2). Semu 2017 describes Ganta, spoken west of Lake Abaya near Arba Minch; the thesis (pp. 13-14) and Hirut 2013 argue that Ganta is the variety Fleming (1976) and Siebert & Hoeft (1994) recorded under the village name 'Kachama' (Kanchama), an East Ometo variety grouped with Zayse, Zargulla, Koorete and Haro, while Bender (2000) and the regional administration since 1994 treated Ganta as a Gamo (North Ometo) dialect. So both works fall within kach1284 (Haro and Kachama/Ganta components respectively), with the Ganta-as-Kachama identification resting on Hirut 2013 and Semu 2017.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for kach1284; this is the first explicit statement, for the Haro variety: tone-accent system, one H per simple word, penultimate default with lexical final-H minority, H migrates to the penult under suffixation. Compatible with Semu 2017 on Ganta (H on final or penultimate mora, lexically fixed).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Haro is a tone-accent (pitch accent) language like Wolaitta, Zayse and Gamo: one high tone per simple word, carried by the syllable nucleus (long vowels take one level tone, never a contour). In disyllabic nominals the H is usually penultimate (bálle 'leaf', kúše 'hand') but a minority have final H (kapó 'bird', kunké 'nose', moló 'fish'), and which is lexical, not predictable. In three-syllable nominals the H is almost always penultimate. Suffixation shifts the H to the new penultimate syllable (gáárma 'lion', gaarm-íe 'lions', gaarm-ié-za 'the lions', p. 31: 'In most cases, the penultimate syllable of a word bears a high tone-accent so that when a suffix gets added to a stem, the high tone-accent occurs on the new penultimate syllable'). Verbs: H placement is set by the paradigm (present tense: root accented; past/future: tense marker accented; imperative: suffix accented, pp. 29-30). H placement distinguishes words: máo 'to dress' vs maó 'cloth', gobá 'be brave' vs góba 'brave' (p. 26). On p. 37 the author states that stress/accent cannot serve as a criterion for the phonological word in Haro because placement depends on lexical and morphological factors. The single mention of 'stress' (p. 37) is in that general remark; the language is described throughout in terms of tone-accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None in simple words (once-per-word constraint). Personal pronouns carry two high tones (táná 'I:ABS', néná 'you:ABS', p. 30), as does the confirmative éró; clitics (tá, né, há, yéé) each bear their own H, so complex words with pronominal or deictic clitics have more than one H (p. 38).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic nominals (šeem, miss, šoš) show a level tone with no H, 'because the domain of tone-accent marking requires at least two syllables' (p. 27); exceptional monosyllabic H-bearing forms are the vocative pronouns dóó and déé, probably borrowed from Bayso (pp. 27, 37); final-H disyllables (kapó, kunké, moló, ašó, wašé, kaatí, laalí, aadé, k'aaré, dees'ó, kumé, addá, p. 28); deverbal nouns may have penultimate (wóss-i 'running') or final (hant-á 'going') H unpredictably (p. 29); once-per-word constraint does not apply to pronouns and some morphologically complex words (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: Hirut 2004 describes Haro (also Haruro; Fleming's 'Geditcho'), spoken on Gidicho island in Lake Abaya; the author reports it mutually intelligible with Ganjule and Gatsame (Kachama) per Haro elders (p. 2). Semu 2017 describes Ganta, spoken west of Lake Abaya near Arba Minch; the thesis (pp. 13-14) and Hirut 2013 argue that Ganta is the variety Fleming (1976) and Siebert & Hoeft (1994) recorded under the village name 'Kachama' (Kanchama), an East Ometo variety grouped with Zayse, Zargulla, Koorete and Haro, while Bender (2000) and the regional administration since 1994 treated Ganta as a Gamo (North Ometo) dialect. So both works fall within kach1284 (Haro and Kachama/Ganta components respectively), with the Ganta-as-Kachama identification resting on Hirut 2013 and Semu 2017.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on placement: both theses describe one high tone per simple word that sits on the penultimate syllable/mora in most nominals and on the final syllable/mora in a lexically fixed minority, with the H moving under affixation. They differ on labelling: Hirut 2004 states outright that Haro is a 'tone-accent language' (pitch accent type, one H per simple word), whereas Semu 2017 uses the term 'tone' throughout for Ganta and explicitly declines to decide whether Ganta is tonal or accentual. Semu's one trisyllabic noun with antepenultimate H (p. 67) contrasts with Hirut's statement that Haro trisyllabic nominals are almost always penultimate (p. 28), but this is one example in a different variety, not a stated rule. Neither work describes the Ganjule variety.
